full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** Confidence is medium-high.

**1. Model family.** This is opinion dynamics, specifically the all-to-all (mean-field) noisy voter model. It is also called the Kirman model or Kirman–Föllmer ant-recruitment model. The noise is spontaneous flipping with probability η. The population-wide shock is a stochastic-resetting or exogenous-shock protocol that sets the magnetization to m₀ = 0.3.

**2. The behaviour in the literature.**
- **Noise threshold without shocks (η ≈ 1/N, one peak versus two).** This is textbook for the noisy voter model.
  - The model's origin is Kirman 1993. The search result confirms the citation (Quarterly Journal of Economics 108, 137–156). It explains herding as the equilibrium distribution of a stochastic process, not switching between multiple equilibria.
  - The 1/N threshold is stated in later papers. For N agents there is a bimodal phase if p<1/(N+1), a flat ("plain") phase at p=1/(N+1), and a unimodal phase above it. Another paper says the unimodal–bimodal transition occurs when the ratio of noise to herding is 1/N. For N = 500 this gives about 0.002, which matches your observed threshold.
  - A recent review of the field shows the same picture. At low noise there are switches between near-consensus states with a bimodal distribution. At high noise the distribution is unimodal. The review is "Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond" (arXiv 2507.11521). Its footnote even mentions a simulation with N=500 all-to-all agents. I did not verify its authors or venue.
- **Shock-induced middle peak, trimodal state, and a rich phase diagram.** This is described directly in a very recent preprint.
  - The preprint is Argany Herrera, Alvarez-Zuzek and Artime, "Opinion dynamics under large-scale exogenous events", arXiv:2609.39858. Authors and title were confirmed on the arXiv abstract page.
  - It applies the framework to the voter model and its noisy version. For the all-to-all noisy voter model under exogenous events, it reports a rich phase diagram with novel trimodal and asymmetric bimodal states.
  - The text describes the trimodal phase as three peaks, at m=±1 and m=m₀. That is your 3 peaks with the extra peak at 0.3.
  - Its noisy-voter definition matches yours: with probability η an agent spontaneously changes opinion, and with probability 1-η a standard voter update occurs.
- **Related, but not the same system.**
  - Trimodal phases also arise in other noisy voter variants without shocks. Examples are the noisy partisan voter model (arXiv 2301.09563) and polarization-induced stress (Physica A, 2024; arXiv 2402.00516). There the central peak comes from a different mechanism, not from resetting.
  - "Voter model under stochastic resetting" (arXiv 2207.08590) resets each voter to its initial opinion, in a 1D, noiseless setting. It is a different protocol.
  - "Noisy voter models in switching environments" (arXiv 2305.19096) is another relative, with a different external-forcing structure.

**3. Caveats.**
- I read only search snippets of the shocks paper, not the full text. I could not check its exact shock definition (reassigning opinions so the mean is exactly m₀) or whether it counts six regimes in the noise-versus-shock-rate plane. The abstract and the trimodal-phase description match closely.
- The shocks paper is a preprint about 34 days old. It is the earliest clear source I found for the shocked behaviour, and I found no earlier one. It is probably not yet peer-reviewed.
- The "six regimes" figure is unverified against the paper. Different regime-counting conventions could change it, but the qualitative result is the same.
- I cited the 1/N threshold from secondary papers, not from Kirman 1993 directly. Related work I know of (Alfarano, Lux and Wagner; Carro et al. 2016) was not retrieved, so I did not cite it.
